British History has many fun stories of colonial officers ‘going full Man Who Would Be King’ (Brooke, Clive, Rhodes etc.) but, lesser known, their American equivalents. Very great ‘You Can Just Do Things’ Antebellum Period Age of Expansion tale

Walker was born in 1824 in Tennessee, coming of age in ‘Manifest Destiny America’. For many ‘sensitive’ types like Walker, the boundary of that destiny did not end at the Pacific Ocean. Latin America was considered fertile ground for Anglo-American expansion. (Importantly here, ‘Anglo’-American expansion). Walker was part of a broader phenomenon known as filibustering - in which private individuals organised unauthorised military expeditions to foreign countries with the aim of overthrowing governments and establishing new regimes favorable to U.S. interests, often with the tacit approval or romantic admiration of American society. Although illegal under US neutrality laws, filibustering was widely tolerated and often celebrated in American public culture

Walker’s first attempt at empire came in 1853 when he led a small band of mercenaries into Baja California and Sonora, territories of Mexico. There, he proclaimed the creation of the “Republic of Sonora,” later renamed the “Republic of Lower California,” and declared himself president. The experiment was a disaster. Lacking supplies, local support and international recognition, Walker’s force dwindled as desertions mounted. He eventually surrendered to US authorities and was tried for violating neutrality laws, but a sympathetic jury acquitted him in minutes. The trial transformed Walker from a failed adventurer into a celebrity, reinforcing his belief that American public opinion was on his side

Undeterred, Walker set his sights on Nicaragua, a country whose internal divisions and strategic importance made it a far more promising target. In the mid-1850s, Nicaragua was locked in a brutal civil war between the Legitimists (conservatives based in Granada) and the Democrats (liberals based in León). Both factions were desperate for military assistance. The Democrats, believing they could control Walker, invited him to bring a small force of American mercenaries to fight on their behalf

In 1855, Walker arrived in Nicaragua with fewer than 60 men, calling themselves “The Immortals.” The name was half-ironic, half-aspirational. They were veterans, drifters, failed professionals, idealists, men fleeing obscurity etc... Some were true believers in Manifest Destiny. Others wanted land or money, some just enjoyed war. Despite their small number, they were well-armed, disciplined and hardened by frontier warfare. Walker quickly demonstrated a talent for command and propaganda. He framed his presence as a defense of liberalism and order, while privately being dismissive of Nicaragua as a ‘joke country’ - instead viewing its territory as the foundation for a new American-dominated state

Walker’s first major victory came at the Battle of La Virgen, where his forces helped secure a key transit route between the Atlantic and Pacific. This route, operated by shipping magnate Cornelius Vanderbilt, was one of the most important commercial corridors in the Americas, allowing travelers to cross Nicaragua as part of the journey between the US East Coast and California. Control of this route gave Walker not only military leverage but economic power

By late 1855, Walker had marched into Granada, the conservative stronghold, and effectively ended the civil war. Though he initially installed a Nicaraguan president to maintain the appearance of legitimacy, it was clear Walker was the true power behind the government. Within months, he maneuvered himself into the presidency through a rigged election, becoming President of Nicaragua in 1856

Once in power, Walker moved quickly to remake Nicaragua in his own image. He declared English an official language alongside Spanish, encouraged American immigration and enacted legal reforms modeled on US law. Most controversially he reinstated slavery, which had been abolished decades earlier, hoping to attract support from Southern states and secure Nicaragua’s future as a slaveholding territory aligned with American interests

These policies alienated nearly every group within Nicaragua. The local population resented foreign domination, land seizures and racial hierarchy. Even former liberal allies realized that Walker had no intention of relinquishing control. His regime relied increasingly on force, executions and censorship to maintain authority

Walker’s actions also provoked powerful enemies abroad. Cornelius Vanderbilt, whose transit company Walker had seized and redistributed to rival businessmen, wanted revenge. Using his immense financial resources, Vanderbilt funded and coordinated regional opposition to Walker. At the same time, neighbouring Central American nations recognised that Walker began to represent an existential threat. This was the beginning of the so-called ‘Filibuster War’

In 1856 and 1857, a Central American coalition formed to destroy Walker’s regime. Costa Rican forces struck first, defeating Walker’s men at the Second Battle of Rivas. Though Walker managed to hold the city, his army suffered heavy losses and was soon ravaged by a devastating cholera epidemic, which killed more soldiers than enemy fire. Disease spread through Walker’s ranks and into Nicaragua’s civilian population, further eroding support

As the coalition tightened its grip, Walker’s supply lines collapsed. Vanderbilt-backed forces cut off the transit route, depriving Walker of reinforcements and revenue. Desertions increased, morale collapsed and Walker’s dream of a permanent American empire in Central America unraveled. In November 1856, facing overwhelming odds, Walker ordered Granada burned to the ground rather than let it fall into enemy hands, leaving behind a sign that read: “Here was Granada”

By May 1857, Walker’s position was untenable. Surrounded by coalition forces and abandoned by most of his allies, he surrendered to the US Navy, which evacuated him from Nicaragua. Remarkably, Walker remained unrepentant though. He returned to the United States a hero to some, especially in the South, where newspapers portrayed him as a martyr to Manifest Destiny. Completely unrepentant, he wrote memoirs defending his actions and continued to plot new expeditions. Despite repeated arrests for violating neutrality laws, he faced little lasting punishment

In 1860, Walker made his final attempt at conquest, landing in Honduras with a small force. This time though circumstances were different. The British Royal Navy, determined to suppress filibustering, captured Walker and handed him over to Honduran authorities. Unlike the United States, Honduras had no interest in trials or symbolic gestures. William Walker was executed by firing squad on September 12, 1860, at the age of 36

A man boards a train in England expecting to reach his stop. He ends up fighting for his life instead. Several passengers stabbed. Armed police swarming the carriages. Two men arrested. Another night of fear in what was once a civilised country.

The attack on the Huntingdon-bound train is not an aberration. It's the latest symptom of a nation that can no longer guarantee the most basic condition of freedom – safety. A train carriage should be the definition of the ordinary: commuters, families, conversation, calm. But Britain has reached a point where the ordinary has become perilous.

The Prime Minister offers condolences, the Home Secretary promises an inquiry, and police issue their sterile statement. We've heard it all before. After every stabbing comes the same hollow ritual: shock, sympathy, and silence. Then nothing changes.

This isn't just about knives. It's about a government that reacts instead of protects, and a culture that tolerates failure as if it were compassion. "Appalling incident," says the Prime Minister. No – what's appalling is that he says it every week. What's appalling is a country that has normalised armed police boarding trains in the dark to stop men butchering strangers.

The deeper crisis is moral. Britain's ruling class has forgotten what government is for. Its first duty is to defend its citizens from harm, not to manage the aftermath. Yet we now live under a state that treats security as a luxury and public fear as a nuisance. Ministers mouth empathy while communities bury the cost.

Whether this attack proves to have a terror link, a migrant connection, or another cause entirely, the principle remains the same: a safe society demands borders, enforcement, and visible authority. A country that cannot control its streets or its trains has ceased to be sovereign in anything but name.

For decades the British people have been told to "stay calm," to "avoid speculation," and to "stand together." But calm is not a policy. Calm does not stop the blood. What's needed is the old logic of civilisation – deterrence, law, consequence. Put police where crime happens. Remove those who threaten the public. Rebuild a justice system that punishes before it apologises.

Every time a citizen is maimed or killed in a preventable attack, it is not just a failure of policing – it is a failure of philosophy. The political class no longer believes in order. It believes in optics. It prefers the illusion of virtue to the reality of safety.

The Huntingdon stabbings should never have happened. Not because such things are unthinkable, but because they were predictable. A state that cannot keep its people safe on a train cannot claim to govern them anywhere else.

Britain's crisis isn't that violence exists. It always has. The crisis is that our leaders have accepted it. And until they stop managing the chaos and start confronting it, there will be more nights like this – more victims, more vigils, more platitudes.
